lead: At the end of his book Ben Sira tells how he sought wisdom from his youth, in prayer before the Temple, and found her. In the Gospel the leaders of the Temple ask Jesus where his authority comes from, and he answers with a question about John the Baptist. Psalm 19 sings that the precepts of the Lord give joy to the heart. The one who seeks wisdom with a pure heart finds her; the one who will not commit himself cannot see the authority standing before him.

r.h: I sought wisdom openly in my prayer
set: Chapter 51 is an appendix to the book: a thanksgiving (vv. 1–12) and a poem about the search for wisdom (vv. 13–30). In Hebrew the poem is an acrostic, each line beginning with the next letter of the alphabet. A Hebrew form of it was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, in the great Psalms Scroll from the eleventh cave at Qumran.
Here the teacher speaks of himself. After a whole book of advice, he tells his students how he himself came to wisdom: young, praying, persevering.
str: vv. 13–14: while still young he prayed for wisdom before the Temple.
vv. 15–17: his heart delighted in her; he made progress and gave glory to God.
vv. 18–20: he resolved to live by her, strove for her, and found her in purity.
kw: In Ben Sira, wisdom is the gift of God that comes to dwell in Israel (24:8) and is found in the Law. She is spoken of as a woman to be loved and sought, not as a set of rules.
Wisdom is not won by study alone. Ben Sira asked for her in prayer before the Temple (vv. 13–14). Solomon too received wisdom by asking (1 Kings 3:9).
“In purity I found her” (v. 20). A clean heart sees clearly. Jesus says the same: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8).
vv: While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.
Ben Sira had travelled (34:12), which in his day was part of a wise man’s education. But the search began earlier, in youth and in prayer.
From the first blossom to the ripening grape my heart delighted in her;
An image of growth over a season. Wisdom is not gained in a day but ripens slowly.
I directed my soul to her, and in purity I found her.
Seeking and finding belong together, as Jesus promises: “search, and you will find” (Matthew 7:7).
ch: The Church sees the fullness of wisdom in Christ, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). The search Ben Sira describes is the search of every young person who prays and asks God how to live. The Catechism teaches that parents have the first responsibility for the education of their children (CCC 2223), and the Church asks pastors and teachers to help them lead the young to prayer and the Word of God. Ben Sira’s story is a quiet encouragement: start young, pray, keep going.

set: The day after the cleansing of the Temple, Jesus is walking in its courts. The chief priests, the scribes and the elders come to him. These three groups formed the Sanhedrin, the high council, and they are the same three groups named in Jesus’ first prediction of his passion (8:31). The question is natural: who gave this Galilean teacher the right to act in the Temple?
This is the first of a series of debates in the Temple (11:27–12:37). Mark presents particular leaders, not the people, many of whom were “spellbound by his teaching” (11:18).
str: vv. 29–30: Jesus’ counter-question about the baptism of John.
vv. 31–32: the leaders reason among themselves.
v. 33: “We do not know”; Jesus will not tell them either.
kw: Not only power, but the right to act. From the start the crowds noticed that Jesus taught with authority, not as the scribes (1:22, 27).
John called Israel to repentance and pointed to the one coming after him (1:7–8). If his baptism was from heaven, then so is the authority of the one he announced.
A reverent way of saying “from God”, as Jews often did out of respect for the divine name, as in Matthew’s “kingdom of heaven”.
vv: By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you this authority to do them?
The answer is hidden in the question. Jesus’ authority comes from the Father who sent him, but they must be willing to see it.
Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin? Answer me.
Teachers of the time often answered a question with a question. Jesus is not evading; he is showing that the answer depends on whether they accepted John.
So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.”
Their answer is not ignorance but refusal. Those who will not commit themselves to the truth they already know cannot receive more.
ch: The Church confesses that Jesus’ authority is that of the Son, sent by the Father: he did not teach as one interpretation among others, but with the authority of the Son (CCC 581). Before Pilate and before the council he will not prove it by force. The scene also teaches honesty in faith: we cannot ask God for new light while refusing the light we have. The Second Vatican Council teaches that all are bound to seek the truth, especially about God and his Church, and to embrace it when they find it (Dignitatis Humanae 1).

rite: St Paul VI (1897–1978), Giovanni Battista Montini, was pope from 1963 to 1978. He guided the Second Vatican Council to its close and put its reforms into practice, including the renewed Roman Missal of 1970. He wrote Humanae Vitae (1968) and Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975), on evangelisation. In December 1964 he came to Bombay for the International Eucharistic Congress, the first pope to visit India. He was canonised in 2018. His memorial falls on 29 May, the day of his priestly ordination in 1920. Like Ben Sira, he sought wisdom all his life, and he used authority as service.
study: When did I first begin to seek God seriously? What helped me then, and what helps me now?
Is there a truth I already know but avoid, saying “I do not know”?
